sections.heading: Why we are writing to you

sentences.text: We represent families affected by IQSEC2-related intellectual developmental disorder.

We are writing because IQSEC2-related intellectual developmental disorder and SLC6A1-related epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizures are placed on the same mechanism road: too little protein from loss of function.
The phenotype similarity score between the two conditions is marked high.
Both gene-disease links are marked definitive in Gene2Phenotype.
For both conditions, the curated mechanism is loss of function, and this is marked as inferred.
The shared informative features listed are atonic seizure, motor seizure, autistic behavior, diagnostic behavioral phenotype, and disinhibition.
Registry design and natural history protocol are marked transferable between the two communities.
Outcome measures and endpoints are also marked transferable, but age of onset and severity still need review before any instrument is adopted.
Clinical networks, sites, and investigators are marked transferable as a starting point.

sections.heading: What we would like to learn from or reuse

sentences.text: We would like to learn from your registry or natural history experience, including the SLC6A1-NDD Prospective Longitudinal Natural History Study and Simons Searchlight.
We would like to understand which outcome measures and endpoints have been practical for your families and investigators.
We would like to learn which clinical sites and investigators are active in your community.
We would also like to study your trial designs as possible templates, because targeted SLC6A1 studies are listed while no targeted IQSEC2 trial was found in the sources searched.
We must not assume the two conditions share the same biology at the level of an individual family's variant.

The mechanism is recorded per gene and disease, not per family, so our own IQSEC2 variant must be confirmed by a clinical geneticist as loss of function, gain of function, or dominant negative before acting on transfer ideas.
The curated mechanisms for both IQSEC2 and SLC6A1 are inferred from variant types, not from functional evidence.
We also must not assume the overlap is deep, because 100% of the shared phenotype weight comes from common low-information terms.
Disease models for SLC6A1 cannot stand in for IQSEC2 models, even if some assay design ideas may be reusable after expert review.
Slipstream does not assert enrolment eligibility for an IQSEC2 family in SLC6A1 trials, so any question about eligibility must go directly to the study team.
The listing for SLC6A1 Connect is marked unverified, so we should not assume it is the right contact or that it runs a registry.
Does the overlap between IQSEC2 and SLC6A1 go beyond common features such as seizures and developmental delay, in your clinical experience?
Is SLC6A1 Connect the right contact, and does it run a registry?
Has our child's specific IQSEC2 variant been functionally classified as loss of function, gain of function, or dominant negative, and does it match the mechanism recorded for the condition?
What functional evidence exists for IQSEC2, given that the curated mechanism is inferred from variant types rather than functional studies?

A study that follows people over time to learn how a condition changes.
A way to track symptoms, function, or change in a study.
The features and symptoms seen in a condition.
